content: Many strategies are employed to address behavioral problems in children, including pharmacological treatments and, more commonly, psychological interventions. These psychological treatments often involve direct engagement with the child and/or their family. Behavioral and cognitive-behavioral therapies have demonstrated efficacy in managing such issues. However, access to these therapies is frequently limited due to barriers such as time constraints and financial costs. Providing parents with the necessary information to address their child's behavioral problems through booklets or other media-based formats could potentially reduce costs and improve accessibility to these interventions. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of media-based cognitive-behavioral therapies for children diagnosed with behavioral disorders, as determined by recognized diagnostic tools. These therapies were compared to standard care and no-treatment control groups. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Biosis, and Sociofile, covering publications up to August 2005. Additionally, bibliographies of selected trials were reviewed, and experts in the field were consulted for further information. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials (e.g., studies employing sequential randomization) that investigated media-based behavioral treatments for children with behavioral problems. Abstracts and titles identified through database searches were screened to determine eligibility. Full-text articles of potentially relevant studies were then assessed by reviewers, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Data from the included studies were analyzed using RevMan 4.2. The review included 11 studies with a total of 943 participants. Overall, media-based therapies for children with behavioral disorders demonstrated moderate, though variable, effectiveness. When compared to no-treatment control groups, effect sizes ranged from -0.12 (95% CI: -1.65 to 1.41) to -32.60 (95% CI: -49.93 to -15.27). When used as an adjunct to medication, effect sizes ranged from -2.71 (95% CI: -5.86 to -0.44) to -39.55 (95% CI: -75.01 to -4.09). Notably, significant improvements were observed when up to two hours of therapist involvement were added to the media-based interventions. The authors concluded that media-based formats for delivering behavioral interventions to caregivers of children with behavioral problems are a valuable option for clinical practice. In some cases, these interventions may be sufficient to produce clinically meaningful changes in a child's behavior. Furthermore, they have the potential to reduce the time primary care providers need to dedicate to each case. Media-based therapies could also serve as an initial step in a stepped-care approach, thereby increasing the number of families who can benefit from these interventions. This, in turn, would free up clinician time to focus on more complex cases. Consequently, media-based therapies have both clinical and economic implications for the treatment of children with behavioral problems.
